cards.title: Which program gets the packet?
cards.body:
The server at `198.51.100.10` runs a website, an email service and a remote login service, all at the same time, all on one IP address.

A packet arrives, addressed to `198.51.100.10`. The address got it to the right computer, but which **program** on that computer should it go to?

cards.title: Ports are flat numbers
cards.body:
Think of a block of flats. The street address gets a letter to the right **building**, and the flat number gets it to the right **door**.

On the internet, the IP address is the building, and a **port** number is the door. Each program listens on its own port, and every packet says which port it's for. You'll often see them written together with a colon: `198.51.100.10:443` means port 443 at that address.

Some ports are standard, so everyone knows where to knock:

- `80`: websites (HTTP)
- `443`: secure websites (HTTPS)
- `53`: DNS
- `22`: remote login (SSH)
- `25`: email between servers (SMTP)

cards.prompt: A port number is stored in **16 bits**. How many different port numbers are possible?
cards.hint: Each extra bit doubles the number of patterns. 8 bits give 256, so 16 bits give 256 × 256.
cards.explanation: 16 bits give 2¹⁶ = 256 × 256 = **65,536** patterns, so ports run from 0 to 65,535. It's the same rule you learned with bytes in Module 1: 8 bits give 256 values, from 0 to 255.

cards.prompt: Match each service to its standard port.
cards.explanation: HTTP uses **80**, HTTPS **443**, DNS **53**, SSH **22** and SMTP **25**. Remember the `#53` in the nslookup output from Module 4? That was the DNS port.

options.text: Port 443: the door for the HTTPS program on that server
A fifth octet of the IP address
The packet can travel up to 443 hops
The server takes 443 milliseconds to answer

cards.explanation: The part after the colon is the **port**. 443 is the standard port for HTTPS, so this means "the secure website program at 198.51.100.10". It isn't part of the IP address, which always has exactly four octets, and it has nothing to do with hops or timing.

cards.title: Your side has a port too
cards.body:
When your laptop connects to `198.51.100.10:443`, it also picks a port for **its own** end of the conversation: a temporary one, usually a high number like `51000`. Replies come back to that port, so they reach the right tab or app.

So a conversation is really identified by **four** numbers: your address and port, and the server's address and port. That's how you can have ten tabs open on the same website without the replies getting mixed up.

cards.title: NAT, the full story
cards.body:
In Module 2 you learned that your home router uses **NAT** to swap private addresses for its public one, and "notes down who asked". Now you can see how it really does that: with **ports**.

When your laptop sends from `192.168.1.20:51000`, the router rewrites the sender as `203.0.113.7:40001`, using its public address and a port it picks. It writes both in its **NAT table**:

- `203.0.113.7:40001` → `192.168.1.20:51000`

The reply comes back to port 40001. The router looks that port up in its table and knows exactly which device, and which port, to pass it to.

cards.prompt: Put the NAT steps in order, now with ports.

items.label: The router changes the sender to 203.0.113.7:40001 and adds it to its NAT table
The router finds port 40001 in its table and passes the reply to 192.168.1.20:51000

cards.explanation: The router rewrites the sender on the way **out** and records it. The server only ever sees `203.0.113.7:40001`, so it replies there. The router then uses the port number to look up which device the reply belongs to.

cards.prompt: On Windows, `netstat -n` lists this computer's connections. Run it and find which **port on the server** `198.51.100.10` this laptop is connected to.
cards.intro:
Microsoft Windows [simulated Command Prompt]
Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.output:
Active Connections

  Proto  Local Address          Foreign Address        State
  TCP    192.168.1.42:51544     198.51.100.10:443      ESTABLISHED
  TCP    192.168.1.42:51547     203.0.113.80:443       ESTABLISHED
  TCP    192.168.1.42:51550     198.51.100.25:22       ESTABLISHED

success.question: Which port on 198.51.100.10 is the laptop connected to?

cards.explanation: The first connection's **Foreign Address** (the other end) is `198.51.100.10:443`, so it's port **443**: a secure website. `51544` is the laptop's own temporary port, under **Local Address**. The last line is a connection to port 22, so this laptop also has a remote login (SSH) open to a different server.

cards.prompt: Two laptops at home both happen to use port **51000** to reach the same website. How does the router keep their replies apart?

options.text: It gives each one a different public port, like 40001 and 40002
It can't, so one laptop's connection fails
It sends every reply to both laptops
The server puts each laptop's private address in its reply

cards.explanation: The router picks a **different public port** for each conversation, so the replies arrive on different ports and its NAT table says which laptop each one belongs to. Nothing fails, nothing is sent to both, and the server never even learns the private addresses.

cards.prompt:
The router's NAT table says:

- `203.0.113.7:40001` → `192.168.1.20:51000`
- `203.0.113.7:40002` → `192.168.1.21:51000`

A reply arrives for `203.0.113.7:40002`. Which device gets it? Type the **last number** of its private address.
cards.explanation: Port **40002** maps to `192.168.1.21:51000`, so the device ending in **21** gets it. Both laptops used port 51000, but the router's different public ports keep them apart.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- A **port** picks which program on a computer gets the data. The IP address is the building, and the port is the door.
- Ports are 16-bit numbers, from **0 to 65,535**. Standard ones: 80 (HTTP), 443 (HTTPS), 53 (DNS), 22 (SSH), 25 (SMTP).
- Your device uses a temporary port for its end of each conversation.
- **NAT** really works with ports: the router gives each conversation its own public port and records it in its **NAT table**.

Next: the two main ways data gets delivered, TCP and UDP.
